analysis.one_liner: Caps U.S. drug list prices at the average of six peer nations, with a tenfold penalty for overcharging.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat without action in the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee since it was introduced on May 5, 2025, with no hearing, vote, or floor action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal to sell a prescription drug or biologic in the U.S. at a list price higher than the average list price for the same drug in Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the United Kingdom. The government would calculate that average each year using prices the drug companies report. Any company that overcharged would owe a fine equal to ten times the price gap, counted for every unit sold. The bill was referred to the Senate Health Committee on the day it was introduced and has sat there since, with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay cash prices or whose insurance leaves them exposed to list prices — uninsured Americans, people with high-deductible plans, and seniors paying full cost before hitting coverage limits — because their out-of-pocket costs are pegged to the U.S. list price, which the bill would force down to the level other wealthy countries pay. Employers and insurers buying drugs at or near list price would also see costs fall. If the caps held, patients could save amounts comparable to what peer-nation price gaps imply for the most expensive biologics and brand-name drugs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured and underinsured patients paying full price

how_it_helps.text: Caps the U.S. list price of each covered drug at the average of what the same drug sells for in Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the United Kingdom, calculated annually by the Secretary of Health and Human Services.

Enforces the cap with a civil monetary penalty equal to ten times the gap between the U.S. list price and the international average, charged per unit sold — large enough to make overcharging unprofitable.

Requires manufacturers to report their list prices in the U.S. and in each of the six countries every year, so the benchmark is based on company-reported data plus public filings rather than estimates.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug and biologic manufacturers, whose U.S. list prices are generally far higher than in peer countries; the bill's tenfold penalty is calculated per unit sold, so a drug priced well above the international average could face enormous total penalties. The bill's text does not address the risk, raised in broader debates over reference pricing, that companies could respond by delaying drug launches in the U.S. or raising prices abroad.

drawbacks.text: The bill controls list prices but not the opaque rebate system between manufacturers and insurers, so savings might show up unevenly for insured patients and more directly for cash-paying and uninsured patients.

Tying U.S. prices to the average of six other wealthy nations could lead manufacturers to launch new drugs later in the United States or raise prices in those six countries, and the bill contains no mechanism to prevent that.

A penalty of ten times the price gap per unit is blunt; a small calculation error or a manufacturer reporting mistake could trigger an enormous penalty, and the bill leaves the details to future regulations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside would be large for the roughly 30 million uninsured Americans and the tens of millions more who pay the full cash price at the pharmacy, since list prices anchor what cash-paying patients owe [S2]. The cost, unpriced in the bill itself, is that drug companies would have a new reason to hold back launches or raise prices abroad, and the bill offers no mechanism to keep other countries from free-riding on American research funding [S2]. The bill also does not address insurance rebates, which sit between list price and what insured patients actually pay. A fair weighing: substantial, direct help at the pharmacy counter, with real but manageable design risks that a serious committee process could address — which is precisely the process this bill has not received.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Health committee, where it has sat without a hearing or vote since May 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Josh Hawley introduced the Fair Prescription Drug Prices for Americans Act on May 5, 2025, joined by Senator Peter Welch.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The committee has taken no recorded action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and it has never reached the Senate floor.

Under the bill, U.S. list prices for covered drugs could not exceed the average list price in Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the United Kingdom, enforced by a penalty of ten times the overcharge per unit sold.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has gone nowhere, drug manufacturers keep charging U.S. patients the highest list prices in the developed world, and nothing has changed for patients paying cash at the pharmacy.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers keep U.S. prices where they are

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and wrote its international reference-pricing cap with the tenfold penalty.

for.name: Sen. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only other member to sign on.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA) and the brand-name drug industry
against.what_they_did: The industry has consistently opposed international reference pricing policies as a group, arguing they would mean foreign governments setting American drug prices; its public posture is the main visible force aligned with keeping the bill from advancing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill is sponsored by a conservative Republican from Missouri and a progressive Democrat from Vermont, but with only two sponsors total its support is thin rather than broad.

industries.note: The bill would cap U.S. list prices at the average of six peer nations — where the same drugs routinely sell for far less — and penalize overcharging at ten times the gap per unit, directly cutting into the highest-revenue market in the world for patented drugs. Ordinary patients benefit; the industry's interest in keeping U.S. prices the global maximum runs against them.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and health insurers
industries.note: The bill regulates list prices but not the rebate and middleman system, so it does not directly cap what these companies extract; savings could flow through existing arrangements unevenly.

analysis.trajectory: Congress is still in session, but the bill has shown no movement since its referral in May 2025 — no hearing, no markup, no additional sponsors beyond its original two. Bills that sit in committee past their first year with two sponsors and no committee action almost never reach the floor. The realistic path to anything happening runs through a bigger drug-pricing package attaching a reference-pricing provision; as a standalone bill, expect it to die quietly at the end of this Congress.
